messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: City Council Member
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 42

He is a 49-year-old European man who has spent much of his adult life trying to look composed in public, and for years he succeeds at that. As a city council member, he knows how to sit through long meetings, answer difficult questions, and appear steady when tensions rise. People in the room often describe him as thoughtful and even-tempered. What they do not see is how much effort it takes for him to hold himself together.

His symptoms begin long before he enters local politics, in the combat zone where he serves as a young man. He does not talk about those years easily, but the memories arrive in fragments: the heat, the dust, the smell of fuel and sweat, the way every sound feels sharpened by the possibility of danger. He remembers the moments before an attack as if the world narrows to the sound of his own breathing. There are days when he still sees one specific scene with painful clarity, as though it is happening again rather than being remembered. At the time, he learns to survive by staying alert, reading every movement, sleeping lightly, and never fully relaxing. Even after the war ends, his body keeps that discipline.

When he returns home, other people expect him to move on. He tries. He marries, builds a family life, and eventually enters public service, a role that seems to suit his seriousness and sense of responsibility. He takes pride in helping his community and being useful. Yet the transition is not smooth. He begins to feel detached from ordinary life, as if he is standing a little apart from everyone else, watching rather than fully participating. Crowded rooms make him uneasy. Sudden loud noises pull him tight inside, his muscles bracing before he can think. He becomes quick to scan exits, windows, and anyone who seems agitated. He tells himself this is just habit, that it is useful to be prepared, but the habit never really turns off.

Over the years, the reminders become harder to ignore. A helicopter overhead, fireworks in the distance, the smell of diesel from a city bus, or a passing siren can all send him back without warning. In those moments he is not only remembering; he is reliving. His heart races, his breathing shortens, and he feels a surge of panic that is embarrassing because it seems to come out of nowhere. He sometimes shuts down in conversation, staring ahead while others wait for his response. At home, his wife notices how often he wakes in the night after a dream he does not want to describe. He says little about it, but he is restless and tired, and sleep no longer restores him. He may drift off on the couch and then jolt awake with his body already prepared for danger.

He tries to keep his work life from being affected, but the cost is visible in the way he carries himself. During contentious council meetings, especially when tempers rise or voices are raised, he feels his chest tighten and his patience shorten. He can become unusually irritable, then immediately regret the sharpness in his tone. Afterward he replays the exchange in his mind, wondering if others noticed how close he came to losing control. He dislikes being in vulnerable positions, dislikes sitting with his back to a door, dislikes anything that makes him feel trapped. He often declines social events that would once have been routine, telling himself he is busy, though the truth is that he is drained by the effort of being alert among people.

He has built a life that looks stable from the outside: marriage, public service, a reputation for reliability. But inside, the war remains organized around his senses and reflexes. He feels guilty at times for how his mind lingers on what he survived, and he is frustrated by how often he cannot simply “let it go,” as others suggest. Still, he continues to show up—to meetings, to family obligations, to the routines of civic life—carrying a tension that never fully leaves him, as if part of him is still back in the combat zone, waiting for the next blast, the next order, the next moment when he has to stay alive.
